source.title: Sparse Autoencoder Insights on Voice Embeddings
source.authors: Dan Pluth; Yu Zhou; V. Gurbani

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE features split as dictionary size increases, using Titanet speaker embeddings and language-label behavior as evidence in a different domain and with a different measure from the original claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a size sweep and describes Spanish-language feature splitting into Spanish-male and Spanish-female latents. It also reports language-classification performance across the sweep. Music identification and feature-steering results do not measure the claimed splitting pattern and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps SAE dictionary size (100–1,200 latents, TopK 5–35) on Titanet speaker embeddings. It reports a single Spanish latent splitting into Spanish-male and Spanish-female latents as size grows. That is a direct V1 result in a new, non-text setting. The SAE method is the original's, not a different method, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs on Titanet speaker embeddings extract monosemantic features that can be identified, steered and split, as in LLM studies. They explicitly claim support for Bricken et al.'s points 1–4, including that features split as the latent space grows. They note their largest latent space is only about 3x the input size.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a linear SAE with TopK activation on 192-dimensional Titanet speaker embeddings, and identifies language features using labeled data and logistic regression. It varies latent dimension and K but does not perform a direct feature-direction comparison with the smaller SAE.
record.method_sensitivity: The latent dimension at which splitting occurs varies with TopK: it rises as K grows up to around 300 latent elements, then plateaus. Language-identification recall also varies across latent dimensions and K values.
record.peer_reviewed: 2025 Conference on Artificial Intelligence x Multimedia (AIxMM)
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates or null controls are reported for the splitting results. The paper's SAE latent dimensions are only approximately 3 times the input dimension at the largest reported scale, and the reported dimension-by-K sweep is summarized partly through figures.
record.rows_left_out: Music-feature identification and the Spanish- and music-feature steering results in Sections V-A2 and V-C were left out because they do not measure splitting as dictionary size increases.

untested.parts: Whether the child latents lie near the parent latent's direction. Whether further splitting happens beyond 300 latents. Only one feature (Spanish) is examined for splitting.
All of it: no large language models and no open SAE releases.
All of it: no nested families and no geometric analysis.
All of it: no parent/child absorption measurement.
All of it: no decomposition of latents across sizes and no count of novel latents.
All of it: no comparison of training objectives.

missing.what: Music-feature recall is 'largely uniform for all SAEs' across the size sweep. This suggests the music latent does not split within 100–1,200 latents, which bears on how general V1 is. rows_left_out excludes this result, but the stated reason (it does not measure splitting) is arguable.
The paper reports no English latent in any SAE; English seems encoded as the default. Only the Spanish feature can be tracked for splitting.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is qualitative: no uncertainty, no controls, and the split comes mostly from figures for a single feature. The K-dependence of the split threshold is not labelled limits_scope, because the split itself recurs at every K. The maximum expansion (about 3x) is far below that of the LLM SAEs.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure whether the resulting feature directions are near the original feature direction.
It does not test large language models or open SAE releases.
It does not test nested concept hierarchies or geometric closeness among split features.
It does not measure parent-child absorption or test whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes it.
It does not compare larger- and smaller-SAE latents as combinations or assess whether larger SAEs add novel latents.
It does not test whether the splitting is an artifact of the sparsity objective or compare objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: Titanet speaker embeddings with SAE
rows.size_stated: SAE latent dimensions 100–1,200 examined; larger values under-trained and omitted
rows.operation_detail: Grid search over latent dimension and TopK value; reported language-classification recall across models.
rows.measure: Recall of the selected latent for Spanish-language identification
rows.value: Recall stabilizes around 70% for most models; lower latent dimensions and higher K values lead to recall in the mid 90’s. The paper attributes two regimes of recall to splitting of the Spanish feature.
rows.note: This is a summary across the grid, not a separately reported value for each dimension and K setting.
rows.check: This is indirect evidence. The roughly 70% recall regime is attributed to male Spanish speakers dropping out of the Spanish latent after the split. The row summarises a grid read from figures, and no per-configuration values are given. 'Partial' understates it: the drop is the signature of the split, not a weak effect.

relation.reason: Reports the Spanish latent splitting into male and female latents as SAE latent size grows.

tranche.reason: The setting is new: non-text Titanet speaker embeddings with a TopK SAE. It gives a direct result on splitting as the dictionary grows. The reader's T2 is not needed, because the method is the original's SAE dictionary learning.

source_check.notes: The splitting evidence is one hand-identified feature (Spanish), shown qualitatively in Fig. 4, with no controls or per-cell numbers; the K/size grid is read from Fig. 2b. The largest SAE is only about 3x the 192-dim input. K for the Fig. 4 series is not restated; index 15 at 200 matches the K=20 model of V-A1.

statements.correction: Authors: the low-recall (~70%) regime is due to the Spanish feature splitting; most male Spanish speakers drop out of the selected latent. The split repeats regardless of K (5–35 examined); the latent size at which it occurs varies.
statements.problem: Numbers match (index 3 at 100, index 15 at 200 with K=20, indices 60/65 at 300, recall about 70%). Minor wording: it is the authors, not only the verdict, who attribute the ~70% regime to the split, with most male Spanish speakers dropping out of the Spanish latent. 'Every K from 5 to 35' is a fair reading of 'regardless of K value', with K 5–35 examined.
Right for this study: the latent size at which the Spanish split occurs varies with K, though the split itself occurs at every K.
Matches V-B: the latent size needed for the split grows with K up to about 300 elements, then plateaus.

statements.correction: Music latent: precision/recall largely uniform across all SAEs examined, with a performance drop at low K (e.g. index 74, K=20, 200 latents: precision 92.3%, recall 99.1%). Splitting of the music feature is not examined.
statements.problem: The Spanish split at 300 is right. The music line overstates the text. The paper says the top music latent's performance (precision and recall, Fig. 3) is largely uniform for all SAEs examined, with a drop at low K. It never examines whether music splits, so music is not shown to be a feature that stays unsplit. '100–1,200' is the examined range, and larger values were omitted as under-trained.

It correctly lists this study as a peer-reviewed reproduction of the qualitative pattern, on Titanet speaker embeddings, by a group not linked to the original (Vail Systems). The largest latent space is only about 3x the input, which the status does not mention, but nothing said is wrong.
